title: The lost wisdom of the Old Moderates
gist: Yglesias rejects a Jacobin claim that corporate publishing consolidation caused reading's decline, arguing books are cheaper than ever and the real cause is competition from endless digital content. The paywalled mailbag portion begins a discussion of public defenders' shift toward ideological work.

insights.claim: Reading has declined because the same technology that made classic literature nearly free also made a bottomless pit of competing content accessible, and attention time is finite, not because publishers made books pricier.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Attention competition, not price, drives media consumption shifts; relevant to how content and platform businesses are valued.

insights.claim: Books have never been cheaper to access: Austen's complete works cost $0.49 and Shakespeare's $0.99 on a smartphone, and hardcovers are cheaper in inflation-adjusted terms.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Undercuts price-based explanations for falling readership; the low-end print market shrank as ebooks displaced mass-market paperbacks.

insights.claim: Zealous defense of every defendant, including the guilty, protects the innocent and is honorable, but Yglesias senses the ideological basis of public-defender work (e.g. DC's Public Defender Service) has shifted.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
entities: Public Defender Service for the District of Columbia
insights.so_what: Signals centrist-left skepticism of criminal-justice activism, relevant to policy drift on crime.
